notes.h: Safe practice in training and performance
notes.b: Sport carries a risk of injury, but much of that risk can be reduced by how people prepare and behave. Safe practice is the name for those habits.
points: Safe practice means the procedures and behaviours that reduce the risk of injury or harm before, during and after physical activity.
In training and performance this includes a warm-up and cool-down, correct technique, and suitable progression and loads, so the body is never asked to do too much too soon.

It also includes supervision by a qualified coach, with rules followed and participants matched by size, age or ability where relevant, so that a smaller or less skilled player is not put at risk by a much stronger opponent.
Intrinsic risk factors come from the performer: fitness level, previous injury, technique and fatigue. For example, a tired player with poor technique is more likely to be hurt.
Extrinsic risk factors come from outside the performer: equipment, playing surface, weather, opponents and coaching. For example, a wet pitch makes slips more likely.
notes.tip: If asked to define safe practice, give the idea (reducing risk of harm before, during and after activity) and then an example. Sort risk factors correctly: from the performer is intrinsic, from outside is extrinsic.

notes.b: When you run a competition or event, the safety of participants, officials and spectators is the organiser's responsibility. Safety is planned in advance, not left to chance.
points: Carry out a risk assessment, a systematic check of the venue and activity to identify hazards and the people who could be harmed, so problems are dealt with before the event.
Arrange first aid cover and an emergency action plan, so casualties are treated and moved quickly.
Use trained stewards and officials, and check facilities and equipment before the event starts.
Set clear rules and give a briefing to participants and officials, so everyone knows what is expected and what to do in an emergency.
Manage crowds and traffic, for spectators and vehicles, so people can enter, leave and be reached by emergency vehicles safely.
Prepare a weather contingency, with hydration points and shelter for participants, so heat, cold or rain does not cause harm.
Set up communication systems between organisers, first aid and emergency services, so help can be called without delay.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe two things organisers should do to keep participants safe, or to examine two approaches at a major event. Pick two from this list and say why each protects people, rather than just naming it.

notes.b: A warm-up is the preparation done just before training or competition. It is built in three phases that move from general to specific, so the body is ready for the exact demands of the activity.
points: Phase 1, pulse raiser: light activity, such as jogging, that gradually increases in intensity to raise the heart rate.
Phase 2, mobility: dynamic stretching (stretching while moving) through the ranges of movement the activity uses, so the joints and muscles are ready for those actions.
Phase 3, activity-specific drills: skill rehearsal that builds up to game intensity, so the performer practises the real movements before they matter.
Mental preparation, such as rehearsing the first passages of play, can be included to focus the performer.
Illustrative soccer warm-up of about 15 minutes: five minutes of jogging, five minutes of dynamic stretches, then five minutes of passing and shooting drills at increasing speed.
notes.tip: When asked to outline the phases or describe a warm-up structure, name the three phases in order and give a named activity with timings, such as the soccer example. Treat the timings as illustrative.

notes.b: Each part of a warm-up has a physical or mental effect. Together they make injury less likely and performance better.
points: It raises heart rate and the temperature of the body and muscles, because warm muscles contract and relax more efficiently.
It increases blood flow and oxygen delivery to the muscles, so they have the fuel they need once work begins.
It improves muscle elasticity and joint mobility, which reduces injury risk because warm, stretchy muscle is less likely to tear.
It rehearses skills and prepares the performer mentally, so they start focused rather than cold.
notes.tip: Exams ask for two benefits of warming up. Give each benefit with its reason, for example raised muscle temperature leading to greater elasticity and lower injury risk.

notes.b: A cool-down is done after activity, and it eases the body back to rest rather than stopping suddenly. Its content mirrors a warm-up in reverse.
points: Content: light activity, such as easy jogging or walking, that gradually reduces in intensity.
Content: static stretching (holding a stretch still) of the muscles used in the activity.
It gradually returns heart rate and breathing to rest, so the body is not left working hard with nothing to do.
It prevents blood pooling (blood collecting in the legs) and the dizziness that can follow stopping suddenly.
It speeds the removal of lactic acid (a waste product that builds up in working muscles) from the muscles.
It may reduce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), the stiffness and ache that can follow hard exercise.
It helps flexibility, because muscles are warm and stretch easily, and it gives time to reflect on the performance.
notes.tip: To outline two reasons for a cool-down, choose from returning heart rate and breathing to rest, preventing blood pooling and dizziness, or removing lactic acid, and give the reason with each.

notes.b: What a performer wears and uses affects both comfort and risk of injury. The right choice protects the performer and the people around them.
points: Footwear should suit the surface and activity: studs for grass and court shoes for indoor courts, so the player has grip without twisting an ankle.
Clothing should suit the conditions, with layers for cold or wet weather, so the performer stays warm and dry.
Jewellery is removed before activity, because it can injure the wearer or others.
Helmets with faceguards are compulsory in hurling under GAA rules, and helmets are worn in camogie, to protect the head and face from the ball and hurleys.
Gumshields protect the teeth and mouth in rugby.
Shin guards protect the lower leg in soccer and hockey.
Buoyancy aids are worn in water activities, so a performer stays afloat if they get into difficulty.
Selection: equipment must be the correct size and fit, and meet approved standards. It should also suit the performer's level, so a racket's grip size and head size are chosen to suit their ability.
notes.tip: When asked why suitable attire and equipment matter, link each item to the injury it prevents. Say that helmets are compulsory in hurling, but only that helmets are worn in camogie.

notes.b: Even well-chosen equipment becomes dangerous if it is damaged or poorly kept. Regular maintenance keeps facilities safe to use.
points: Nets, posts and goals are inspected and repaired regularly, and goals must be secured in place.
Surfaces are checked for holes, debris and other hazards before use, so players do not trip or twist an ankle.
Pool water quality is tested and maintained, so swimmers are not exposed to harmful bacteria or chemicals.
Proper storage keeps equipment clean, dry and undamaged.
Maintenance prevents injury, keeps equipment effective and extends its life.
Example: an unsecured goal can topple onto a player, so securing it before each session prevents that injury.
notes.tip: Exams ask how to maintain a facility and why. Name one facility, say what you check or repair, and give the injury it prevents, as in the goalpost example.

notes.h: Types of injury: acute, chronic, sprain and strain
notes.b: Injuries are grouped by how they start and by the tissue damaged. Knowing the groups helps you name an injury correctly and treat it.
points: Acute injury: sudden onset, such as a sprain, strain, fracture, dislocation, concussion or cut.
Chronic (overuse) injury: develops gradually from repeated stress, such as tendinitis, shin splints, stress fracture or tennis elbow.
Sprain: damage to a ligament, the tissue that joins bone to bone, for example an ankle sprain from landing awkwardly.
Strain: damage to a muscle or tendon, the tissue that joins muscle to bone, for example a hamstring strain from sprinting without a warm-up.
notes.tip: A sprain is a ligament injury and a strain is a muscle or tendon injury. Examiners test this, so do not swap them.

notes.b: Each activity has injuries that happen again and again, because of the movements and contact it involves. Knowing the cause shows how to prevent the injury.
points: Soccer: ankle sprain, caused by landing awkwardly, which twists the ankle and overstretches a ligament.
Soccer: hamstring strain, caused by sprinting without a warm-up, when cold muscle is stretched too fast.
Rugby: concussion, caused by a collision or tackle that shakes the brain inside the skull.
Rugby: shoulder dislocation, caused by a heavy tackle or a fall onto the shoulder, which forces the joint out of its socket.
notes.tip: You are asked for two common injuries in a named activity, with their causes and first aid. Choose one activity, name both injuries, give the cause of each, then the treatment.

notes.b: Soft-tissue injuries, such as sprains and strains, swell and bleed under the skin. PRICE is a five-step routine that limits this damage in the first 48 to 72 hours.
points: PRICE stands for Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression and Elevation, and is used in the first 48 to 72 hours after a soft-tissue injury.
Protect: remove the player from the activity and guard the injured area from further damage.
Rest: stop using the injured part, since movement can make the injury worse.
Ice: a cold pack wrapped in cloth and applied in short periods, never directly on the skin, to reduce pain and swelling.
Compression: an elastic bandage applied firmly, but not so tight that it cuts off circulation.
Elevation: raise the injured limb above heart level to reduce swelling.
Avoid heat on a fresh soft-tissue injury, because it increases swelling.
Refer for medical assessment if the injury is severe.
notes.tip: Never recommend heat on a fresh soft-tissue injury. When asked for first aid treatment, give each PRICE letter with what you do and why.

notes.h: Assessing an injury on the field (SALTAPS)
notes.b: Before deciding whether an injured player can carry on, a coach or first aider needs a quick, orderly check. SALTAPS gives the steps in order.
points: SALTAPS stands for See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active movement, Passive movement and Strength.
See: watch how the player fell and how they move.
Ask: ask what happened and where it hurts.
Look: check for swelling, bruising or deformity (a joint or limb that looks the wrong shape).
Touch: feel the injured area for tenderness.
Active movement: the player moves the joint themselves.
Passive movement: the examiner moves the joint while the player relaxes.
Strength: the player pushes or pulls against resistance. Pain, weakness or instability at any step means the player should not return to play.
notes.tip: SALTAPS is used to decide whether the player can continue. Learn the seven words in order, and state that pain, weakness or instability at any step means no return to play.

notes.b: Two injuries need special rules because they can be serious or can spread infection: a blow to the head and an open wound.
points: Concussion signs: confusion, headache, dizziness, loss of consciousness and balance problems.
Concussion can occur without loss of consciousness, so a player who stays awake may still be concussed.
Remove the player from play immediately and do not return them that day. The guidance is: if in doubt, sit them out.
Medical clearance is needed before a graduated return to play, meaning a step-by-step return rather than straight back to full play.
Cuts and bleeding: apply pressure with a clean dressing, wearing gloves, to stop the blood and protect the helper from infection.
Blood rule: the player leaves the field until the bleeding stops.
notes.tip: Do not give return-to-play timelines in days for concussion. Say medical clearance and a graduated return.

notes.b: Training makes you fitter only when the body has time to recover. Without that recovery, more training makes performance worse, which is overtraining.
points: Overtraining: training too hard or too often without enough recovery, so performance declines.
Symptoms: persistent fatigue, a raised resting heart rate and poor sleep.
Symptoms: frequent illness and injury, because a tired body is less able to resist infection or cope with stress.
Symptoms: loss of motivation and irritability.
Symptoms: falling performance and muscle soreness that does not go away.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define overtraining and give symptoms. Include the idea that recovery is missing, so performance declines, then list several symptoms.

notes.h: Designing training schedules to avoid overtraining
notes.b: A good schedule balances work and recovery. These principles keep the load rising without pushing the athlete into overtraining or fatigue.
points: Progress gradually: a common rule of thumb is to raise weekly load by about 10%, which is guidance rather than a law.
Build in rest days and easy weeks so the body can recover.
Periodisation, alternating harder and easier blocks of training, is one way to plan recovery into a schedule.
Vary intensity so that not every session is maximal.
Monitor load with session RPE (how hard the athlete rates the session) multiplied by session duration, heart rate or a wellness questionnaire.
Adequate sleep and nutrition support recovery between sessions.
Listen to the athlete: reduce load when they report fatigue or pain.
notes.tip: To explain two ways a schedule can prevent overtraining, choose two principles, such as gradual progression and rest days, and say how each allows recovery.

notes.b: Evaluating a schedule means judging it against those principles and then suggesting improvements. You look for where load rises too fast or recovery is missing.
points: Check where weekly load rises sharply, since a sudden jump increases injury and overtraining risk.
Check whether the schedule includes rest days and easy weeks, and whether intensity varies, because a plan with every session hard gives no time to recover.
Propose changes that smooth the jump, add rest or vary the intensity.
notes.tip: When evaluating a schedule, identify where load jumps too quickly or recovery is missing, then propose a specific change for each problem.

keyTerms.definition: Procedures and behaviours that reduce the risk of injury or harm before, during and after physical activity.
A risk that comes from the performer, such as fitness level, previous injury, technique or fatigue.
A risk that comes from outside the performer, such as equipment, playing surface, weather, opponents or coaching.
A systematic check of a venue and activity to identify hazards and the people who could be harmed.
A structured series of activities that prepares the body and mind for performance and reduces injury risk.
The first warm-up phase, light activity that gradually raises the heart rate.
Light activity followed by static stretching that gradually returns the body to rest after performance.
An injury with a sudden onset, such as a sprain, strain, fracture or concussion.
An injury that develops gradually from repeated stress, such as tendinitis or shin splints.
Damage to a ligament, the tissue that joins bone to bone.
Damage to a muscle or tendon, the tissue that joins muscle to bone.
The first-aid method for soft-tissue injuries: protect, rest, ice, compression and elevation.
A sequence of checks used on the field to decide whether an injured player can continue.
Training too hard or too often without enough recovery, so that performance declines.

questions.prompt: Describe a warm-up structure athletes can use to prepare for performance, and outline two reasons for including a cool-down.
questions.model: Phase 1, pulse raiser: light jogging that gradually increases in speed, to raise the heart rate and the temperature of the body and muscles. Phase 2, mobility: dynamic stretches such as leg swings and lunges through the range of movement the sport uses, which improves muscle elasticity and joint mobility. Phase 3, activity-specific drills: passing and shooting drills that build from walking pace to match intensity, so skills are rehearsed and the athlete is mentally ready. Reason 1 for a cool-down: light activity gradually returns the heart rate and breathing to rest, which prevents blood pooling in the legs and dizziness after stopping suddenly. Reason 2: it speeds the removal of lactic acid from the muscles and may reduce muscle soreness, while the static stretching that follows helps flexibility.

questions.prompt: Identify two injuries common in a named physical activity, their causes, and the first aid treatment for one.
questions.model: Activity: soccer. Injury 1: ankle sprain, a ligament injury caused by landing awkwardly after a jump or tackle. Injury 2: hamstring strain, a muscle injury caused by sprinting without a warm-up. First aid for the ankle sprain uses PRICE. Protect: the player leaves the pitch and the ankle is guarded from further twisting. Rest: the player stops weight-bearing activity. Ice: a cold pack wrapped in cloth is applied in short periods, never directly on the skin, to reduce pain and swelling. Compression: an elastic bandage is applied firmly but not so tight that it cuts off circulation. Elevation: the ankle is raised above heart level to reduce swelling. Heat is avoided, and a player with severe pain or an inability to bear weight is referred for medical assessment.

questions.prompt: Define overtraining and outline two ways a training schedule can be designed to prevent it.
questions.model: Overtraining is training too hard or too often without enough recovery, so performance declines despite continued effort. First, progress the load gradually, using the common rule of thumb of raising weekly load by about 10%, so the body adapts rather than being overloaded suddenly. Second, build in rest days and easy weeks, and vary the intensity so that not every session is maximal, allowing recovery between hard efforts.
